title: The Fick equation: flow times extraction
goal: Use the Fick equation to link cardiac output, arterial and venous O₂ content and VO₂, and explain why training raises VO₂max mainly through a bigger cardiac output.

steps.title: The Fick equation, both sides
steps.text:
The heart module gave you the [Fick principle](g:fick-principle): VO₂ = Q × [a-vO₂ difference](g:a-vo2-difference). Now you can fill in the difference itself [[c:fick-vo2max]]:

**VO₂ = Q × (CaO₂ − CvO₂)**

- Q: [cardiac output](g:cardiac-output), L·min⁻¹;
- CaO₂: arterial O₂ content, from the last lesson, mL·L⁻¹;
- CvO₂: O₂ content of [mixed venous blood](g:mixed-venous-blood): all the body's returning blood, mixed in the pulmonary artery.

L·min⁻¹ × mL·L⁻¹ gives mL·min⁻¹. Use mL per **litre**: content in mL·dL⁻¹ must be multiplied by 10 first.

The share of arriving O₂ that the body takes out is the [extraction fraction](g:o2-extraction): (CaO₂ − CvO₂) ÷ CaO₂ [[c:extraction-def]].

claims.text: By the Fick equation, VO₂max is the product of maximal cardiac output and the arterial to mixed venous O₂ difference.

evidence.quote: According to the Fick equation, V ˙ O 2max is determined by the product of the maximal cardiac output ( Q ˙ max ) and the arterial to mixed venous O 2 difference ( a - v ¯ O 2 difference).

claims.text: Systemic O₂ extraction fraction is the a-vO₂ difference divided by arterial O₂ content.

evidence.quote: the systemic O ¯ 2 extraction fraction—ie, the fraction of O 2 that is taken up with respect to the amount available for utilization ( a - v ¯ O 2 difference/CaO 2 )

steps.title: A runner at rest
steps.problem: A 70 kg runner sits at rest. Cardiac output is 5 L·min⁻¹, CaO₂ 200 mL·L⁻¹ and mixed venous CvO₂ 150 mL·L⁻¹. Find her VO₂ and extraction fraction.
steps: Per kg: 250 ÷ 70 = 3.6 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, inside the usual resting range of 3–5.
Extraction = 50 ÷ 200 = 25%: three quarters of the O₂ goes back to the heart unused. That is a big reserve.

steps.title: From rest to maximum
steps.text:
From rest to VO₂max, VO₂ rises about 15-fold. Both terms of the Fick equation rise:

| | rest | maximum |
|---|---|---|
| Q (L·min⁻¹) | about 5 | about 20–40 |
| a-vO₂ difference (mL·L⁻¹) | about 50 | about 120–170 |
| extraction | about 25% | up to about 90% |

In pooled data from 17 studies, Qmax rose about 5–6 L·min⁻¹ for every extra 1 L·min⁻¹ of VO₂max, and the a-vO₂ difference at max rose from 118 to 168 mL·L⁻¹ between VO₂max values of 2 and 4.5 L·min⁻¹ [[c:fick-pooled]]. Extraction climbs to about **90%** and then stops rising [[c:extraction-90]].

So the pump can still grow a lot; the a-vO₂ difference is near its ceiling.

claims.text: In pooled individual data, Qmax rose 4.9–6.0 L·min⁻¹ per 1 L·min⁻¹ of VO₂max, and the a-vO₂ difference rose from 118 to 168 mL·L⁻¹ between VO₂max values of 2 and 4.5 L·min⁻¹, then fell.

evidence.quote: Q˙max and two-LBF increased linearly by 4.9-6.0 L · min-1 per 1 L · min-1 increase in V˙O2max (R2 = .73 and R2 = .67, respectively; both P < .001). The a-v¯O2 difference increased from 118-168 mL · L-1 from a V˙O2max of 2-4.5 L · min-1 followed by a reduction

claims.text: Systemic O₂ extraction fraction rises with VO₂max to about 90% and then plateaus; leg extraction approaches 90–95%.

evidence.quote: systemic O2 extraction fraction increased up to ~90% (V˙O2max: 4.5 L · min-1) with no further change
Likewise, leg O2 extraction fraction increased with V˙O2max to approach a maximal value of ~90-95%

steps.title: The same runner at VO₂max
steps.problem: At VO₂max the same runner reaches a cardiac output of 25 L·min⁻¹. CaO₂ is 200 mL·L⁻¹ and CvO₂ falls to 40 mL·L⁻¹. Find her VO₂max and how each term changed from rest.
steps: VO₂max = 25 × 160 = 4,000 mL·min⁻¹ = 4.0 L·min⁻¹, or 57 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ at 70 kg.
Extraction = 160 ÷ 200 = 80%. There is little left to squeeze out of each litre; most of any further gain must come from more flow.

steps.title: What training changes: mostly the pump
steps.text:
When VO₂max rises with training, which term grew? A [meta-analysis](g:meta-analysis) of 13 training studies (130 untrained or moderately trained young adults, 5–13 weeks) found VO₂max and Qmax both rose, but the a-vO₂ difference at max did not change significantly [[c:training-qmax]]. That fits the classic view: in whole-body exercise, delivery is the main limit [[c:delivery-primary]].

Not everyone agrees that extraction stays put. Most studies *calculate* the a-vO₂ difference from VO₂ ÷ Q, so any error in measuring Q lands in it, and small studies can't detect a small change. And CaO₂ tends to fall in the fittest, which hides a rise in extraction [[c:extraction-hidden]].

claims.text: After 5–13 weeks of endurance training in untrained or moderately trained young adults, VO₂max and Qmax increased but the a-vO₂ difference at maximal exercise did not change significantly.

evidence.quote: After data pooling, V˙O2max (SMD = 0.75, P < 0.0001) and Qmax (SMD = 0.64, P < 0.0001), but not a-V˙O2diff at maximal exercise (SMD = 0.21, P = 0.23), were increased after ET.

claims.text: O₂ delivery, not muscle O₂ extraction, is viewed as the primary limit to VO₂max in whole-body exercise, and the training gain in VO₂max comes mainly from a higher maximal cardiac output.

evidence.quote: the increase in VO2max with training results primarily from an increase in maximal cardiac output (not an increase in the a-v O2 difference)
Thus, O2 delivery, not skeletal muscle O2 extraction, is viewed as the primary limiting factor for VO2max in exercising humans.

claims.text: Calculating the a-vO₂ difference from VO₂max ÷ Qmax adds measurement error, small studies are underpowered, and lower CaO₂ in the fittest can mask higher extraction; the fittest had about 10% lower CaO₂.

evidence.quote: First, when the a - v ¯ O 2 difference is calculated by the Fick equation, a large variation is introduced as a result of measurement error in Q ˙ max , especially when non‐invasive methods are used.
individuals with the highest V ˙ O 2max displayed a substantially lower CaO 2 (~10%) than those with a low V ˙ O 2max

debate.question: Does endurance training raise VO₂max through more O₂ extraction, or almost only through a bigger cardiac output?

sides.position: Almost only through cardiac output: in pooled training studies Qmax rose and the a-vO₂ difference at max did not change; delivery is the main limit.
Extraction contributes too: the fraction extracted rises with VO₂max to about 90%, and training studies are too noisy and small to see a modest change in the a-vO₂ difference.

steps.title: The muscle could take more
steps.text:
If delivery is the main limit, the muscle should be able to use more O₂ when it gets more. It can. When a small muscle mass, such as one thigh in knee-extension, gets far more blood per kg than in cycling, its O₂ uptake per kg is much higher [[c:small-muscle]].

Yet the periphery isn't irrelevant. In 6 men cycling at VO₂max while breathing less O₂, VO₂max fell in step with venous PO₂: a sign that diffusion from capillary to muscle also limits uptake [[c:tissue-diffusion]].

The likely picture: delivery sets most of the ceiling, diffusion trims it. The last lesson of this module looks at the muscle end; the VO₂max module weighs the limits in full.

claims.text: When a small muscle mass is overperfused during exercise, it has an extremely high capacity for consuming O₂, which supports delivery as the main limit in whole-body exercise.

evidence.quote: when a small muscle mass is overperfused during exercise, it has an extremely high capacity for consuming oxygen

claims.text: When men cycled at VO₂max breathing 21%, 15% and 12% O₂, VO₂max fell linearly with femoral and mixed venous PO₂ through the origin, suggesting tissue diffusion limitation of VO₂max.

evidence.quote: Each of the PO2 variables was linearly related to VO2max (r = 0.99 each), with an intercept not different from the origin.
we conclude that tissue diffusion limitation of VO2max may be present in normal humans

points: Fick: VO₂ = Q × (CaO₂ − CvO₂), with content in mL·L⁻¹ so that L·min⁻¹ × mL·L⁻¹ gives mL·min⁻¹.
Extraction fraction = a-vO₂ difference ÷ CaO₂: about 25% at rest, up to about 90% at VO₂max.
From rest to max, Q rises about 5-fold and the a-vO₂ difference about 3-fold; VO₂ about 15-fold.
Training raises VO₂max mainly through Qmax; whether extraction adds a little is debated, partly because it is hard to measure.
A small, overperfused muscle can use far more O₂ than in whole-body work: delivery is the main limit, diffusion a smaller one.

variants.stem: From rest to VO₂max, a cyclist's O₂ uptake rises about 15-fold. Which mix of the Fick terms best explains that?

options.text: Cardiac output about ×5, a-vO₂ difference about ×3
options.why: Right: 5 × 3 = 15. Both terms rise; flow has more room to grow.
The a-vO₂ difference rises a lot too, from about 50 to 150 mL·L⁻¹ or more.
Extraction can't rise 15-fold: at rest it is already about 25%, and the ceiling is about 90%.
Arterial content barely changes; it may even fall slightly in hard exercise.

variants.stem: A triathlete goes from rest to an all-out effort. Her VO₂ goes from 0.25 to 3.75 L·min⁻¹. Which change in the Fick terms fits best?

options.text: Q from 5 to 25 L·min⁻¹, a-vO₂ from 50 to 150 mL·L⁻¹
Q from 5 to 75 L·min⁻¹, a-vO₂ fixed at 50 mL·L⁻¹
options.why: No human heart pumps 75 L·min⁻¹; the a-vO₂ difference also rises.

options.text: Q fixed at 5 L·min⁻¹, a-vO₂ from 50 to 750 mL·L⁻¹
options.why: Blood holds only about 200 mL·L⁻¹, so the a-vO₂ difference can't reach 750.

options.text: Q from 5 to 15 L·min⁻¹, a-vO₂ from 50 to 100 mL·L⁻¹
options.why: 15 × 100 = 1,500 mL·min⁻¹: well short of 3,750.

variants.stem: At VO₂max a runner's cardiac output is 30 L·min⁻¹, CaO₂ 190 mL·L⁻¹ and mixed venous CvO₂ 30 mL·L⁻¹. What is her VO₂max?

options.why: This is Q × CaO₂: the O₂ delivered, not the O₂ taken up. It forgets the venous O₂ that returns.
This treats the a-vO₂ difference as 16 mL·dL⁻¹ without converting to mL·L⁻¹ (factor 10).
This is Q × CvO₂: the O₂ that goes back to the heart unused.

variants.solution: a-vO₂ = 190 − 30 = 160 mL·L⁻¹. VO₂max = 30 L·min⁻¹ × 160 mL·L⁻¹ = 4,800 mL·min⁻¹ = 4.8 L·min⁻¹.

variants.stem: At VO₂max an elite cyclist's cardiac output is 35 L·min⁻¹, CaO₂ 185 mL·L⁻¹ and mixed venous CvO₂ 25 mL·L⁻¹. What is his VO₂max?

options.why: This is Q × CaO₂ (6,475 mL·min⁻¹): delivery, not uptake.
This treats the a-vO₂ difference as 16 mL·dL⁻¹ without converting to mL·L⁻¹.
This is Q × CvO₂ (875 mL·min⁻¹): the O₂ that returns unused.

variants.stem: At VO₂max a triathlete's cardiac output is 22 L·min⁻¹, CaO₂ 195 mL·L⁻¹ and mixed venous CvO₂ 45 mL·L⁻¹. What is her VO₂max?

options.why: This is Q × CaO₂ (4,290 mL·min⁻¹): delivery, not uptake.
This treats the a-vO₂ difference as 15 mL·dL⁻¹ without converting to mL·L⁻¹.
This is Q × CvO₂ (990 mL·min⁻¹): the O₂ that returns unused.

variants.stem: A lab report gives a cyclist's maximal a-vO₂ difference as 16 mL·dL⁻¹ and his cardiac output as 25 L·min⁻¹. What is his VO₂max?

options.why: Right: 16 mL·dL⁻¹ = 160 mL·L⁻¹; 25 × 160 = 4,000 mL·min⁻¹.
This multiplies 25 × 16 without converting dL to L: a factor of 10 too low.
This multiplies by 100 instead of 10 (1 L = 10 dL); no one has a VO₂max of 40 L·min⁻¹.

variants.solution: 16 mL·dL⁻¹ × 10 = 160 mL·L⁻¹. VO₂max = 25 L·min⁻¹ × 160 mL·L⁻¹ = 4,000 mL·min⁻¹ = 4.0 L·min⁻¹.

variants.stem: A runner's VO₂max is 4.2 L·min⁻¹ and her maximal cardiac output 28 L·min⁻¹. What is her a-vO₂ difference at max?

options.why: Right: 4,200 mL·min⁻¹ ÷ 28 L·min⁻¹ = 150 mL·L⁻¹.
This is the value in mL·dL⁻¹ given the wrong unit: 150 mL·L⁻¹ = 15 mL·dL⁻¹.
This divides Q by VO₂ (28 ÷ 4.2): the inverse.
This keeps VO₂ in L·min⁻¹ (4.2 ÷ 28): that gives litres of O₂ per litre of blood, not mL.

variants.solution: a-vO₂ = VO₂ ÷ Q = 4,200 mL·min⁻¹ ÷ 28 L·min⁻¹ = 150 mL·L⁻¹.

variants.stem: A cyclist's VO₂max is 5.4 L·min⁻¹ and his maximal cardiac output 32 L·min⁻¹. What is his a-vO₂ difference at max?

options.why: This is the value in mL·dL⁻¹ given the wrong unit: 169 mL·L⁻¹ ≈ 17 mL·dL⁻¹.
This divides Q by VO₂ (32 ÷ 5.4): the inverse.
This keeps VO₂ in L·min⁻¹ (5.4 ÷ 32): that gives litres of O₂ per litre of blood, not mL.

variants.solution: a-vO₂ = VO₂ ÷ Q = 5,400 mL·min⁻¹ ÷ 32 L·min⁻¹ = 168.75 ≈ 169 mL·L⁻¹.

variants.stem: At VO₂max a trained rider has CaO₂ 200 mL·L⁻¹ and mixed venous CvO₂ 30 mL·L⁻¹. What is his systemic extraction fraction?

options.why: This is CvO₂ ÷ CaO₂: the share that goes back unused.
This divides CaO₂ by the a-vO₂ difference (200 ÷ 170); a fraction can't exceed 100%.
This is the a-vO₂ difference in mL·L⁻¹ read as a percentage.

variants.stem: A runner at rest has CaO₂ 200 mL·L⁻¹ and mixed venous CvO₂ 150 mL·L⁻¹. What is her systemic extraction fraction?

options.why: This is CvO₂ ÷ CaO₂: the share that goes back unused.
This divides CaO₂ by the a-vO₂ difference (200 ÷ 50); a fraction can't exceed 100%.
This is the a-vO₂ difference in mL·L⁻¹ read as a percentage.

variants.stem: A previously untrained runner raises her VO₂max by 12% over 10 weeks. According to pooled training studies, which Fick term most likely made the difference?

options.why: Right: in pooled studies Qmax rose with VO₂max, while the a-vO₂ difference at max did not change significantly.
In the meta-analysis the a-vO₂ difference at max didn't rise significantly after 5–13 weeks.
Training doesn't raise CaO₂; it may even lower it as plasma expands.
Resting HR isn't a Fick term at max; it falls with training but doesn't set VO₂max.

variants.stem: Elite cyclists extract a larger share of arterial O₂ than moderately trained riders, yet their a-vO₂ difference at max is often similar. Best explanation?

options.text: Their CaO₂ is lower, so a bigger share of a smaller amount
options.why: Right: the fittest had about 10% lower CaO₂; a higher fraction of less O₂ gives a similar difference.

options.text: Their mixed venous O₂ is higher, as muscles waste more
options.why: Higher extraction means lower venous O₂, not higher.

options.text: Their cardiac output is lower, so blood stays longer
options.why: Elite riders have much higher Qmax, not lower.
Systemic extraction rises with VO₂max to about 90%.

variants.stem: A meta-analysis found no significant change in the maximal a-vO₂ difference after training. A coach concludes muscle adaptations can't raise VO₂max at all. Best judgement?

options.text: Too strong: small, noisy studies could miss a modest rise in extraction
options.why: Right: the a-vO₂ difference is mostly calculated from VO₂ ÷ Q, so Q's error lands in it, and studies were small.

options.text: Correct: no significant change proves no change
options.why: Non-significant is not the same as zero, especially with 130 people across 13 small studies.

options.text: Wrong: the meta-analysis found a large rise in extraction
options.why: It found a small, non-significant effect (SMD 0.21) on the a-vO₂ difference.

options.text: Correct: muscle adaptations only matter below VO₂max
options.why: They matter most below VO₂max, but that doesn't rule out a small effect at max.

variants.stem: In one-leg knee-extension, the working thigh gets far more blood per kg than it does in cycling, and its O₂ uptake per kg is much higher. What does this show about VO₂max in cycling?

options.text: In cycling the muscle gets less O₂ than it could use
options.why: Right: given more flow, the same muscle uses far more O₂, so in whole-body exercise delivery limits it.

options.text: In cycling the muscle's mitochondria set the limit
options.why: If mitochondria set the limit, more flow wouldn't raise uptake per kg so much.

options.text: Knee-extension uses a different fibre type
options.why: It is the same quadriceps; the difference is flow per kg of muscle.

options.text: The heart is stronger in knee-extension
options.why: Cardiac output is far lower in knee-extension; flow is shared by much less muscle.

variants.stem: The meta-analysis behind 'training raises Qmax, not the a-vO₂ difference' pooled 13 studies of 130 untrained or moderately trained young adults over 5–13 weeks. What most limits applying it to a well-trained triathlete's next season?

options.text: It tells us about early gains in untrained people, not trained athletes
options.why: Right: short programmes in untrained people may not show what happens after years of training.

options.text: A meta-analysis is weaker evidence than one large study
options.why: A good meta-analysis usually ranks above a single study.

options.text: 13 studies is too many to combine
options.why: Combining more studies adds precision; the issue is who was studied.

options.text: Training can't raise VO₂max in trained people
options.why: It still can, more slowly; the issue is whether the same mechanisms apply.
